title: A Gallery of Waves
intro: Seven periodic signals, each with its series, its spectrum and a measure of how fast the harmonics add up to the wave. The pattern to look for: what the signal looks like, jumps, corners or neither, tells you how its harmonics fall.

blocks.text: How to read each entry

Every signal below is set up in the viewer with a preset. For each one the page gives what the wave looks like, its series (using $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T$ and $A_k$, $\varphi_k$ in the form of the Fourier Series: Building a Wave (#/math/fourier-transform/fourier-series) page), how its harmonics fall, and the RMS gap between the wave and the sum of harmonics $0\ldots N$ as the viewer's readout reports it. All values are for $T = 1$ s, so harmonic $k$ sits at $k$ Hz. As the Convergence and the Gibbs Phenomenon (#/math/fourier-transform/convergence) page explained, a signal with jumps has $A_k \sim 1/k$, one with corners but no jumps has $A_k \sim 1/k^2$, and the error goes down accordingly.
Square wave

$+1$ for the first half of the period and $-1$ for the second. Series: $\frac4\pi[\sin\omega_0 t + \frac13\sin3\omega_0 t + \frac15\sin5\omega_0 t + \cdots]$. Only odd harmonics, $A_k = 4/(\pi k)$: 1.2732, 0.4244, 0.2546, 0.1819 at $k = 1, 3, 5, 7$, all with phase $-90^\circ$. The power is 1, of which the fundamental has 81.1%. The jumps make it slow: the RMS gap is 0.2245 at $N = 7$ and still 0.1006 at $N = 39$, and the sum overshoots each jump to 1.1792, the Gibbs horn.
Look for odd-numbered ribbons only (the even ones lie flat) and bars on the right wall falling like 1/k. Press Add harmonics and watch the sum square up while the horns at the jumps stay high.
Sawtooth wave

A ramp from $-1$ up to $+1$, then a drop. Series: $\frac2\pi[\sin\omega_0 t - \frac12\sin2\omega_0 t + \frac13\sin3\omega_0 t - \cdots]$. Every harmonic is present, $A_k = 2/(\pi k)$: 0.6366, 0.3183, 0.2122, 0.1592 for $k = 1\ldots4$, with the phase alternating between $-90^\circ$ (odd $k$) and $+90^\circ$ (even $k$). Power $\frac13$. It has one jump per period, so it converges like the square wave: RMS gap 0.1642 at $N = 7$ and 0.0716 at $N = 39$. The peak of the 39-harmonic sum is 1.1539, which is 0.179 above the ramp's own value of 0.975 at that point: the Gibbs overshoot, measured from the local height of the signal.

The jumps are at $t = \pm T/2$, half-way between the centre and each edge of the picture. Turn to Turn −90 to see the spectrum: bars at 1, 2, 3, ... Hz, each the reciprocal fraction of the first: 0.64, 0.32, 0.21, ... Compare the phase panel with the square wave's, where every phase was −90°. Here they alternate.
Triangle wave

Straight lines from $+1$ down to $-1$ and back. Series: $\frac{8}{\pi^2}[\cos\omega_0 t + \frac19\cos3\omega_0 t + \frac1{25}\cos5\omega_0 t + \cdots]$. Odd harmonics, $A_k = 8/(\pi^2k^2)$: 0.8106, 0.0901, 0.0324, 0.0165 for $k = 1, 3, 5, 7$, all phase 0. No jumps, so it converges quickly: the RMS gap is 0.0102 at $N = 7$ and 0.0009 at $N = 39$. The fundamental alone has 98.6% of the power; harmonics up to $k = 3$ have 99.8%.

With N = 7 the sum cannot be told from the dashed triangle at this size; the readout says the RMS gap is 0.0102. The ribbon at $k = 3$ is a ninth as tall as the first, and the later ones are barely there.
Pulse train

A pulse of height 1 and width 0.5 s, repeating every $T$ seconds. At $T = 1$ it is a 50% duty cycle: $A_0 = 0.5$ and $A_k = 2d\operatorname{sinc}(kd)$ with $d = 0.5$, which is 0.6366, 0, 0.2122, 0, 0.1273 for $k = 1\ldots5$, the odd harmonics alternating in sign (phase 0 or $180^\circ$ for $k = 3$, since $\operatorname{sinc}(1.5) < 0$). Even harmonics vanish because the 2 Hz zero of the envelope falls on them. It has jumps, so the RMS gap is 0.1122 at $N = 7$, 0.0503 at $N = 39$, and at $N = 39$ the peak is 1.0896, a Gibbs overshoot of 8.96% of the jump (here 1). For a longer period the spectrum fills in under the same sinc envelope, as on the From Series to Transform (#/math/fourier-transform/series-to-transform) page: at $T = 4$ the duty is 12.5% and $A_1\ldots A_4$ are 0.2436, 0.2251, 0.1961, 0.1592.

In this side view you see the spectrum: stems at 1, 3, 5, 7 Hz and nothing at 2, 4, 6. Raise Period to 2 and stems appear at every multiple of 0.5 Hz; the one at 2 Hz is zero, the envelope's first null. Raise it to 4 and the stems are 0.25 Hz apart, under the same dashed envelope.
Half-wave rectified sine

The top halves of a sine wave, with the bottom halves cut to 0. Series: $\frac1\pi + \frac12\sin\omega_0 t - \frac2\pi[\frac13\cos2\omega_0 t + \frac1{15}\cos4\omega_0 t + \cdots]$. The average is $1/\pi = 0.3183$, the fundamental is exactly half: $A_1 = 0.5$, and then only even harmonics survive, $A_2 = 0.2122$, $A_4 = 0.0424$, $A_6 = 0.0182$; $A_3 = A_5 = 0$. There is a corner where each hump starts, but no jump, so the coefficients fall as $1/k^2$ (the formula is $2/(\pi(k^2 - 1))$). Power $\frac14$. RMS gap: 0.0098 at $N = 7$, 0.0008 at $N = 39$.

The odd ribbons beyond the first are flat. The fundamental, a pure sine, is the biggest oscillating ribbon (bar 0.5), but the constant term (the bar at 0 Hz, 0.318) is more than half as large: without it, the flat stretches between the humps would sit at $-0.318$ instead of 0.
Full-wave rectified sine

The absolute value of a sine, with one hump per period (so the fundamental is the hump rate, not the underlying sine's). Series: $\frac2\pi - \frac4\pi[\frac13\cos\omega_0 t + \frac1{15}\cos2\omega_0 t + \frac1{35}\cos3\omega_0 t + \cdots]$, with $A_0 = 0.6366$ and $A_k = 4/(\pi(4k^2 - 1))$: 0.4244, 0.0849, 0.0364, 0.0202 for $k = 1\ldots4$, all with phase $180^\circ$. Power $\frac12$. Of the six with an infinite series it converges fastest (the RMS gap is 0.0063 at $N = 7$ and 0.0005 at $N = 39$), because its harmonics fall as $1/k^2$ with a small constant, about $1/(\pi k^2)$. A power supply uses this: the 'ripple' after a rectifier is the harmonics at $k \ge 1$, which is why the first one (0.424 against the 0.637 average, two-thirds of it) is the one a smoothing capacitor is chosen against.

From the side: a bar of 0.637 at 0 Hz, then 0.424, 0.085, 0.036, 0.020, 0.013, ... at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 Hz. The first oscillating bar is only two-thirds the DC bar, and the rest are tiny. Lower N to 3 and the RMS gap is still only 0.0197.
Two tones

$\cos\omega_0 t + 0.5\cos(3\omega_0 t + 60^\circ)$: the signal built in the Sinusoids and Complex Exponentials (#/math/fourier-transform/sinusoids) page, where the series is the whole signal, with exactly two lines, $A_1 = 1$ with phase 0 and $A_3 = 0.5$ with phase $60^\circ$. Power $\frac12 + \frac{0.25}2 = 0.625$. Because the series is finite, the gap is zero once $N \ge 3$; before that it is the missing third tone.

At N = 3 the sum is the signal and the RMS gap in the readout is 0. Drop N to 2 and the third harmonic disappears from the sum; the gap becomes the third tone's RMS, $0.5/\sqrt2 = 0.3536$. Add Delay 0.1: the phases become −36° and −48° and the amplitudes are unchanged.
Side by side
At the same number of harmonics the signals separate into three groups by how smooth they are. RMS gap at $N = 7$:

items: With jumps: square 0.2245, pulse train 0.1122, sawtooth 0.1642. Coefficients fall as $1/k$; the Gibbs horn is 8.95% of the jump.
Continuous, with corners: triangle 0.0102, half-wave rectified sine 0.0098, full-wave rectified sine 0.0063. Coefficients fall as $1/k^2$.
A finite number of lines: two tones, 0 for $N \ge 3$.

blocks.text: Power in the first harmonics, as a fraction of the total at $N = 3$: square 0.9006, sawtooth 0.8275, pulse train 0.9503, triangle 0.9977, half-wave 0.9953, full-wave 0.9992. Reading a spectrum, then, is also a way of reading a waveform: if the bars drop off quickly, the wave is smooth.
Practice

blocks.title: Which signal is it?
blocks.text: A periodic signal with $T = 1$ has $A_0 = 0.5$ and bars $A_1 = 0.6366$, $A_2 = 0$, $A_3 = 0.2122$, $A_4 = 0$, $A_5 = 0.1273$. Which signal of the gallery is it, and does the sum overshoot at jumps?
solution: The constant term of 0.5 and the first odd bars match the 50% pulse train: $A_k = 2d\operatorname{sinc}(kd)$ with $d = 0.5$ gives $0.6366$, 0, $0.2122$, 0, $0.1273$. The bars fall as $1/k$, so there are jumps, and the sum overshoots by 8.95% of the jump, which is 1: peak about 1.09.
blocks.answer: The 50% pulse train; yes, a peak near 1.09.

blocks.title: Predict the decay
blocks.text: Without the formula, how will the harmonics of a wave that looks like a sawtooth but with its drop rounded into a smooth curve decay compared with the sawtooth's $1/k$?
solution: Rounding the drop removes the jump, leaving a continuous wave, so the coefficients will eventually fall faster than $1/k$: like $1/k^2$ if there are corners, faster if it is smoother. The first few harmonics may look similar, since they describe the broad shape, but the high-$k$ tail is where the jump showed itself. The Gibbs horn also disappears.

blocks.title: Power budget
blocks.text: For the half-wave rectified sine, what share of the total power is in the constant and first harmonic together?
solution: Total power is $\frac14$. The constant has $A_0^2 = (1/\pi)^2 = 0.1013$ and the fundamental $A_1^2/2 = 0.125$. Together 0.2263, or $0.2263/0.25 = 90.5\%$. Adding $A_2$ (power $0.2122^2/2 = 0.0225$) takes it to $0.2488$, or 99.5%.
